lead: When a load is connected to a fixed source, a very small load resistance takes a large current but little voltage, and a very large one takes a large voltage but little current. Somewhere between, the load power is greatest. The maximum power transfer theorem says where: a load takes the most power from a fixed linear network when the load resistance equals the network's Thevenin resistance, RL = Rth, and that power is Vth²/(4Rth). Communication circuits, sensors and antennas are designed for it; power systems deliberately avoid it, because at the maximum-power point half the power or more is lost.
prereq: You need: Thevenin's and Norton's theorems and the power formula P = I²R.

sections.h3: Load power from a Thevenin source

blocks.text: Reduce the fixed network to V<sub>th</sub> in series with R<sub>th</sub> and connect a load R<sub>L</sub>. One current flows round the loop, I = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>), so the load power is

where Vth is in volts, Rth and RL in ohms and PL in watts. At RL = 0 the load is a short and takes no power (no voltage). As RL grows very large the current falls towards zero and the power falls with it. The power is positive in between, so it has a peak. For the network of Thevenin's and Norton's theorems (24 V, 4 Ω) the load powers are 23.04 W at 1 Ω, 32 W at 2 Ω, 36 W at 4 Ω, 32 W at 8 Ω and 23.04 W at 16 Ω (Figure 2.5.1).

sections.h3: Proof: the peak is at R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>

items: Hold V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> fixed and differentiate P<sub>L</sub> with respect to R<sub>L</sub> by the quotient rule: dP<sub>L</sub>/dR<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²[(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)² − 2R<sub>L</sub>(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)]/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)⁴.
Cancel one factor (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>): dP<sub>L</sub>/dR<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²(R<sub>th</sub> − R<sub>L</sub>)/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)³.
Set it to zero: R<sub>th</sub> − R<sub>L</sub> = 0, so R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>.
It is a maximum: the derivative is positive for R<sub>L</sub> below R<sub>th</sub> (power rising) and negative above it (power falling).

blocks.text: In Norton form the same result reads P<sub>max</sub> = I<sub>N</sub>²R<sub>N</sub>/4. Two loads give equal power on either side of the peak when their product is R<sub>th</sub>²: 2 Ω × 8 Ω = 16 = 4² in the figure. The curve is flat near its top, so a load within about a factor of two of R<sub>th</sub> still takes close to 90 % of P<sub>max</sub> (32 of 36 W).

sections.h3: Maximum power is not maximum efficiency

blocks.text: In the equivalent circuit the source delivers V<sub>th</sub>I and the load takes I²R<sub>L</sub>, so the efficiency is η = R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>). At the maximum-power point η = 50 %: as much power heats R<sub>th</sub> as reaches the load. A large load gives a high efficiency but little power.

Two cautions. First, the 50 % belongs to the equivalent circuit only; the real network can waste more, because the theorem says nothing about its internal losses (worked example 1 finds 26.5 %). Second, the theorem fixes the source and varies the load. If the load is fixed and the source resistance can be chosen, the load power is greatest with the smallest possible source resistance, not with R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>L</sub>.

So the theorem fits weak-signal circuits, where every microwatt counts: an antenna feeding a receiver, a microphone feeding a preamplifier, a solar panel driven to its maximum power point. Mains supplies and power stations are built for high efficiency, with source resistance far below the load. For AC sources the condition becomes the conjugate match ZL = Zth* (see applying network theorems to AC circuits).

examples.question: The network of worked example 1 in Thevenin's and Norton's theorems (32 V source, 4 Ω series, 12 Ω across, 1 Ω to terminal a) has V<sub>th</sub> = 24 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω. Find the load for maximum power, the maximum power, the efficiency of the equivalent circuit, and the true efficiency of the original network at that load.
steps: Maximum power needs R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω.
P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) = 24²/16 = 576/16 = 36 W. Check: I = 24/(4 + 4) = 3 A and 3² × 4 = 36 W.
Equivalent circuit: the 24 V source delivers 24 × 3 = 72 W, so η = 36/72 = 50 %.

Original network with the 4 Ω load: the load branch is 1 + 4 = 5 Ω, in parallel with 12 Ω: 5 × 12/17 = 3.53 Ω. The source sees 4 + 3.53 = 7.53 Ω and supplies 32/7.53 = 4.25 A, that is 32 × 4.25 = 136 W.
Load current from the current divider: 4.25 × 12/17 = 3 A, so the load takes 36 W, matching the equivalent.
True efficiency: 36/136 = 26.5 %. The other 100 W heats the 4 Ω, 12 Ω and 1 Ω inside the network.
examples.answer: R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω, P<sub>max</sub> = 36 W; 50 % in the equivalent circuit but only 26.5 % in the real network.

examples.question: The network with a controlled source in Thevenin's and Norton's theorems (worked example 2) has V<sub>th</sub> = 9 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω. Find the maximum power any load can take, and compare it with the power in a 6 Ω load.
steps: R<sub>th</sub> must come from the test-source or V<sub>oc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub> method because of the controlled source: R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω.
6 Ω load: I = 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A, P = 1² × 6 = 6 W, about 89 % of the maximum.
Had the controlled source been wrongly switched off (R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω), the predicted best load would be 4 Ω; the true power in 4 Ω is 81 × 4/49 = 6.61 W, short of 6.75 W.
examples.answer: R<sub>L</sub> = 3 Ω takes 6.75 W; a 6 Ω load takes 6 W.

traps: Saying maximum power transfer gives maximum efficiency. At R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> the equivalent circuit is only 50 % efficient, and the real network can be worse.
Using P = V<sub>th</sub>²/R<sub>L</sub>. The load voltage is not V<sub>th</sub>; at the peak it is V<sub>th</sub>/2.
Choosing R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>L</sub> when the load is fixed and the source resistance is the variable. Then the best source resistance is the smallest one.
Finding R<sub>th</sub> with a dependent source switched off. The best load then comes out wrong (4 Ω instead of 3 Ω in worked example 2).
Using R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> for an AC source with reactance. The condition there is the conjugate match.

quiz.q: State the maximum power transfer theorem for a DC network.
quiz.a: A load takes maximum power from a fixed linear network when R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>; the power is then V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>).

quiz.q: Why does the load power fall to zero both for a short-circuit load and for a very large load?
quiz.a: With R<sub>L</sub> = 0 the load voltage is zero, so V × I = 0. As R<sub>L</sub> grows very large the current tends to zero, so I²R<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)² falls like V<sub>th</sub>²/R<sub>L</sub>.

quiz.q: A network has V<sub>th</sub> = 20 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 5 Ω. Find the best load and the maximum power.
For the 24 V, 4 Ω source of worked example 1, which two loads each take 32 W?
quiz.a: Solve 576R/(4 + R)² = 32: R² − 10R + 16 = 0, so R = 2 Ω or 8 Ω. Their product is 16 = R<sub>th</sub>².

quiz.q: A source has V<sub>th</sub> = 10 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 2 Ω. Compare load power and efficiency for R<sub>L</sub> = 2 Ω and R<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω.
quiz.a: 2 Ω: I = 2.5 A, P = 12.5 W, source power 25 W, η = 50 %. 8 Ω: I = 1 A, P = 8 W, source power 10 W, η = 80 %. The larger load is more efficient but takes less power.

quiz.q: A 10 Ω heater is fixed and you may choose the series resistance of the 50 V supply anywhere from 0 to 10 Ω. Which value gives the heater the most power?
quiz.a: 0 Ω: the heater power 2500 × 10/(R<sub>s</sub> + 10)² is largest when R<sub>s</sub> is smallest, 250 W. R<sub>s</sub> = 10 Ω would give only 62.5 W.

quiz.q: In worked example 1 the equivalent circuit says 50 % but the network is 26.5 % efficient at the same load. Which number is the real one and why?
quiz.a: 26.5 %. The Thevenin equivalent matches the network only at the terminals, so it gives the right load power (36 W) but not the power wasted inside, which depends on how the network is built (136 W drawn from the 32 V source).

beyond: Solar inverters run a maximum power point tracker that keeps adjusting the panel's load so it stays at the top of its power curve as sunlight changes. Radio engineers match an antenna to a receiver with networks of inductors and capacitors, and low-noise amplifier design trades the power match against the best noise match. Search for 'MPPT perturb and observe', 'impedance matching network' and 'noise figure versus power match'.

figure.caption: Load power from the Thevenin source of worked example 1 (24 V, 4 Ω), computed for loads from 0 to 20 Ω. The power peaks at 36 W when the load equals 4 Ω, and 2 Ω and 8 Ω both give 32 W. The dashed curve is the efficiency of the equivalent circuit, only 50 % at the peak and rising towards 100 % for large loads.

spec.aria: A curve of load power against load resistance rising from 0 to a peak of 36 W at 4 ohm and falling to 23 W at 16 ohm; points at 2 ohm and 8 ohm, both 32 W; a dashed efficiency curve rising from 0 through 50 percent at 4 ohm.
